cases.question: How would you decide what to cache in front of our pricing service?
answers: We cached the assembled response for the forty hottest SKUs and left everything else uncached, because the memory to hold the tail was worth more as headroom than as hit rate. skill.name: Idempotent design
skill.assessment_scope: Designing capture and retry paths a duplicate request cannot double-charge.

cases.question: Walk me through designing payment capture so a retry cannot charge twice.
answers: Idempotency is really important in payments. Payments are one of those areas where correctness matters more than almost anywhere else, because money is involved and customers notice immediately when something goes wrong. An idempotent operation is one that can be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the first application, which is the standard definition. In a payments context that means a capture should only ever charge the customer once, no matter how many times the request is sent. Retries happen for all sorts of reasons — network timeouts, client bugs, users double-clicking — so you have to design for them from the start rather than bolting something on later. The way this is usually done is with an idempotency key, which is a value that identifies the request so the server can tell whether it has seen it before. Most payment providers support this and it is considered a best practice across the industry. It is also worth saying that testing this properly matters, because a bug here is expensive.
cases.reason: One hundred and eighty words that define idempotency twice, explain why payments matter, and never say what they would build or what they have built. Length is not depth: this is the same finding as the short definition in dd-direct-01, at eight times the word count.

cases.question: How would you decide what to cache in front of our pricing service?
answers: Caching is one of those topics where there is a lot to think about. The first thing I would say is that caching is a trade-off, and you always have to think about the trade-offs. There is the question of what to cache, and the question of how long to cache it for, and the question of when to invalidate it, and all three of those questions interact with each other. You also have to think about consistency, because a cache is by definition a second copy of the data and second copies can disagree with the first one. In general my approach would be to look at the data and the access patterns and then make a decision based on what I find, because every system is different and what works in one place may not work in another. skill.name: Idempotent design
skill.assessment_scope: Designing capture and retry paths a duplicate request cannot double-charge.

cases.question: Walk me through designing payment capture so a retry cannot charge twice.
answers: You key the request so a repeat is recognisable rather than reprocessed.
On our side the key is derived from the order id, and the intent row goes in inside the same transaction as the response, so a crash between the two cannot leave a charge with no record of it.

The one that actually bit us was two attempts inside the same millisecond. The unique index rejected the second, and we changed the handler to treat that violation as a duplicate rather than a failure, because the alternative is a customer being told a payment failed when it had gone through.
probes: How is that key produced and stored on your side?
What happens when two of them arrive at the same instant?
cases.reason: The ladder was walked and the candidate climbed it: definition, then the mechanism they built, then the concurrency failure and the handler decision with its customer consequence. Both figures are deep_probed, which is the combination that must be reachable without being automatic.

depth_reconciliation.why: No disagreement between the datasets, the label and the stated gold evidence; confirmed against the rubric without change.

skill.name: Database performance
skill.assessment_scope: Diagnosing and improving database performance broadly.

task.name: Make a slow query fast
task.description: Diagnose and fix a slow query.

cases.question: A report that used to take two seconds now takes forty. How do you find out why?
answers: I'd start with whether the data grew or the query changed.
Same query and parameters against the replica first, to separate the query from the load, then the plan next to the one it used to have.

Last time the plan had flipped to a sequential scan because a bulk import left the statistics stale. The hint that would have fixed the symptom was the wrong fix — it hides the cause and the next query with that shape breaks the same way — so ANALYZE went into the import instead.
probes: How would you tell those two apart?
And when you find it, what do you change?
cases.reason: Three rungs, each adding something: a fork, a method, then a root cause with the rejected fix and why it was rejected. Deep by the failure-mode-of-the-fix argument, on a debugging task with no architecture in it.

depth_reconciliation.why: The hint that fixes the symptom is rejected because it hides the cause and the next query of that shape breaks the same way: a failure mode that changed the remedy.

answers: Match on the provider reference first, then amount and date.
Unmatched rows went to a suspense account rather than being written off, with the reason as a required field.
